headline: Every move costs a child something. Plan it with them.
intro: Training that helps your team plan each move between homes and schools with the child, not around them.

problem.scene: Tuesday: Leah, 11, is told she moves on Friday.
problem.question: She packs her things into bin bags. On Thursday she throws a chair.
without: Moves arranged around a free bed
No time to prepare the child
The details that help get lost
with: A school place arranged at the same time
A handover on what helps them settle
problem.standards: The Care Planning, Placement and Case Review (England) Regulations 2010 and the education guidance expect a school place arranged alongside a new home, and protection for moves in years 10 and 11.
problem.evidence: Developmental trauma is explained honestly: what it is, and that it is not a recognised diagnosis in DSM-5 or ICD-11, nor a label for a child.

groups: Social workers, personal advisers and independent reviewing officers
Foster carers, supervising social workers and residential staff
Designated teachers, pastoral staff and virtual school staff
Health and early help staff who stay through a move
notes: Best with social care and schools together

outcomes: See a move from their side
Describe a move from the child's side: the weeks before, the day itself and the first week.
Recognise the signs that a move is bringing back earlier losses, before and after it happens.
Explain what developmental trauma is and isn't, and how threat shapes stress, learning and behaviour.
Use Bowlby, Ainsworth and Pauline Boss's ambiguous loss to explain why children test new adults.
Plan a move with the child
Use a transition planning tool covering goodbyes, belongings, the school place and the first week.
Write a short handover for the new carers and school on what helps the child settle.

pillars.title: The Secure Base model
pillars.stance: What helps a child feel safe in a new home
pillars.stance_line: Five things carers do, used to plan the first week after a move.
items: Helping the child trust that the adult will be there.
Helping the child make sense of and manage their feelings.
Building the child's self-esteem by accepting who they are.
Helping the child feel effective and part of decisions.
Helping the child feel they belong.
pillars.base: Developed by Gillian Schofield and Mary Beek at the University of East Anglia.

facilitator.name: Luke Rodgers BEM
facilitator.line: From care leaver to care leader
paras: Luke went into care at 10. He has spent his career inside children's services as a consultant, trainer and keynote speaker, and is CEO of The Care Leaders.

He has worked with councils and the NHS nationally on children who move between systems, including Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent, where more than 400 staff across health, social care and education were trained.
He led the national engagement on England's new fostering standards for the Department for Education, so he knows what the standards expect of the adults around a child.
He was a Knowledge Equity Fellow at Saïd Business School, University of Oxford, and was awarded the British Empire Medal in 2018 for commitment to children and families.
